implementation_notes: Scala's default collections are immutable and a case class is immutable data with a copy method, so the query shape is the ordinary one: a method returns a new value without being told to. The official Scala book defines a pure function as one whose output depends only on its inputs and its implementation, and flags Unit-returning methods as the usual sign of an impure one - useful as a review heuristic. Use var and mutable collections only inside identity-bearing objects and keep the command methods that touch them small. This is the realization for any non-effect-system Scala codebase, including Java-interop-heavy ones.
code_sketch:
final case class Money(amount: BigDecimal, currency: String):
  def scaled(factor: BigDecimal): Money = copy(amount = amount * factor)   // query

def total(lines: List[Line]): BigDecimal =
  lines.foldLeft(BigDecimal(0))((acc, l) => acc + l.price.amount * l.qty)
pitfalls: Case-class fields are vals but can still hold mutable values (Array, mutable.ListBuffer), and copy() is shallow.
Java interop and null: a method that looks total and pure can throw a NullPointerException on a null from Java, which is an effect.
Unit-returning methods signal command intent; calling one from inside a query hides a side effect behind an innocuous-looking call.

variants.name: effect-typed IO with Cats Effect (side effects as values)
variants.idiom_name: IO[A] values describe effects; referential transparency preserved
variants.implementation_notes: The effect-system realization keeps the same split but makes effectful operations values: Cats Effect documents IO as a data type for encoding side effects as pure values that preserves referential transparency, so logic composes IO (and Either) with map/flatMap and the only impure call is the runtime at the edge of the program. Choose it when the project already runs a Typelevel stack and effects must be visible in the types; it is a whole-program decision, not a local style, so the immutable-collections variant remains the right default elsewhere.
variants.code_sketch:
def totalCents(lines: List[Line]): IO[BigDecimal] =          // pure description, nothing runs yet
  IO.pure(lines.foldLeft(BigDecimal(0))((acc, l) => acc + l.price.amount * l.qty))

val program = totalCents(lines).flatMap(n => IO(println(n)))  // effect suspended, performed at run
pitfalls: IO.pure evaluates its argument eagerly: wrapping a side-effecting expression in IO.pure performs it at construction; use IO(...) / IO.delay to suspend.
A map/flatMap callback that performs an effect outside the IO (printing, mutating a var) breaks referential transparency even though the types still say IO.
Mixing IO into a few methods while the rest of the codebase performs effects directly loses the guarantee the types advertise.
